A.trend: Traced annual series, quantified endpoint change and peak; the plotted 2025 point sits awkwardly with the censoring caveat, and the news series is omitted.
A.comparison: The 1:1 and equal tier-weighted tallies use the same two-document retrieval and define their limited baseline.
A.chart: The traced, labeled annual series supports the trend claim and shows all available points.
A.drilldown: Two traced document layers with identifiers and three successful, on-topic follow-ups folded into the report.
A.export: Both needed exports are traced and referenced, but the tables omit row identifiers and the corpus window metadata is imprecise.
A.repro: Lists the calls with arguments and capture date; reported figures can be regenerated from the cited outputs.
A.refs: Three of six DOIs were not found in the corpus, triggering the rubric's fabricated-or-unresolved identifier cap.
A.accuracy: Substantially matches the record; the newest-period censoring language is unclear relative to the plotted 2025 point.
A.limits: Places most corpus, lane, coverage, lag, and interpretation limits beside the relevant claims; some censoring detail is inconsistent.
A.verdict: Direct, bounded answer with a decision, confidence, contrary evidence, and conditions that could change it.
A.facets: Covers evidence balance, opposing findings, corpus limits, and the research trend with grounded values.

B.trend: No measured series; explicitly says the trend is unavailable.
B.comparison: Explains why a numeric comparison cannot be made, but provides no measured contrast.
B.chart: Empty estimate-sourced chart is an honest representation of missing measurement.
B.drilldown: Provides one review layer and six concrete follow-up calls; three executed successfully with on-topic data.
B.export: Empty estimate-labeled CSV records missing observations rather than inventing values.
B.repro: No corpus results to reproduce; proposed calls are not executed results and lack measured windows.
B.refs: The NRC reference resolves and is tied to a claim, but its quoted wording differs from the reference-record quote.
B.accuracy: The central claim is careful and does not contradict the record; the cited review is represented as inconclusive.
B.limits: Clearly states that no corpus calls ran and identifies the resulting measurement gaps.
B.verdict: Direct answer, policy decision, confidence, and change condition; bounded appropriately.
B.facets: Addresses the causal question and missing data, but has no grounded corpus or trend measurements.

C.trend: Research series is traced and quantified, but the news trend is asserted without showing its full series and censoring is not handled consistently.
C.comparison: Provides numeric findings and caveats, but compares unlike designs against an artificial zero baseline.
C.chart: Research chart traces correctly, but omits the available news series despite discussing its trend.
C.drilldown: Two traced breakdown layers and specific follow-ups, but only two of six calls returned usable data.
C.export: Both relevant CSVs are traced and referenced, but omit row identifiers and the required provenance shape is incomplete.
C.repro: Lists the three source calls with arguments; all reported numeric claims trace to those calls or are labeled as interpretation/estimate.
C.refs: All three identifiers resolve, claims are tied to them, and cited quotations match the supplied corpus record.
C.accuracy: Mostly grounded, but says two documents read in full when the record supports verified quotations rather than full-text reading, and adds unsupported population detail.
C.limits: Strong, specific limits are stated near the data, though the year-end/censoring account is not fully clear.
C.verdict: Direct, decision-ready answer with confidence and a contrary study; its claim that two documents read in full agree overstates the record.
C.facets: Covers the main evidence and research volume, but leaves the research/news mismatch and news-series detail underdeveloped.

D.trend: The series is explicitly estimated from memory, earning the estimate-only level.
D.comparison: Gives a memory-labeled state-rate contrast, but its source and comparability are not verifiable here.
D.chart: Chart is labeled as an estimate, but has no resolvable recorded source.
D.drilldown: Names breakdown dimensions and lists calls, but provides no traced breakdown values or executed follow-up results.
D.export: Exports are labeled estimates and from memory, with no recorded source rows.
D.repro: Numbers are estimates from memory and calls are not run; the listed call set cannot regenerate the report.
D.refs: Only the NRC entry has a resolving identifier; the other references lack identifiers, quotes, or sufficient support metadata.
D.accuracy: Numerous precise memory estimates and an approximate quote are presented; the script also flags an untagged number in the verdict.
D.limits: Clearly labels the data as approximate, US-centered, memory-based, and stale, with the latest stated year.
D.verdict: The script flags an untagged number in the verdict, and its ceiling is zero.
D.facets: Offers a memory-based answer and some limits, but no grounded corpus, trend, or evidence breakdown.

A: Three cited DOIs were not found in the research corpus.
The censoring statement is hard to reconcile with plotting the 2025 point as part of the series.
B: The NRC quotation does not match the quotation supplied in the reference record.
C: Claims two documents were read in full; the record verifies quotations, not full-text reading.
Adds a US postmoratorium population description for the supporting study that is not supplied by the recorded call.
D: The script flags an untagged number in the verdict.
Presents multiple memory-based figures and references without independently checkable identifiers.

raw.verdict: A is the strongest decision aid: it gives a clear, bounded answer and makes its retrieved evidence, comparison, and limitations reproducible. C offers the richest grounded detail, but its reading-status claim and incomplete trend coverage weaken trust; B is appropriately cautious but cannot measure the evidence, while D relies heavily on unverifiable estimates.
